From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability

Dmitry Scherbakov ††thanks: Core contributors. Correspondence to: scherbakovdv@my.msu.ru    Oleg Chernikov11footnotemark: 1    Victoria Khamash11footnotemark: 1    Kirill Afendulev Affiliation: Alexey Dontsov,  Ivan Oseledets,  Elena Tutubalina,  Anton Korznikov
Abstract

We study feature vectors: directions in a language model’s activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.

1 Introduction

The linear representation hypothesis posits that large language models (LLMs) encode human-interpretable concepts (e.g., sentiment or truthfulness) as linear directions in its activation space (Mikolov et al., 2013; Park et al., 2023; Elhage et al., 2022). When such direction is tied to a pre-specified concept, we call it a feature vector. These vectors can serve two complementary roles. Projecting activations onto a feature vector, called probing, measures how active its concept is in a given context (Alain & Bengio, 2016; Belinkov, 2022); adding it to the activations, called steering, pushes generation toward that concept (Subramani et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024). Both techniques are highly effective in practice and have been used for safety-critical LLM monitoring and control (Zou et al., 2023a; Bergen et al., 2026; Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

But how can we get these feature vectors? Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024; Templeton et al., 2024) attempt to recover all atomic features a model might store, yet a growing body of evidence shows SAEs fail to faithfully find true model features and underperform simpler baselines on downstream tasks (Wu et al., 2025; Korznikov et al., 2026; Smith et al., 2025). Another option is to define the concepts we care about in advance and extract their directions from contrastive pairs: for each concept, we gather texts that express it and texts that express its opposite, then take the difference between their mean activations. The resulting difference-in-means vector is more robust and interpretable than SAE features, but requires matched data per concept, limiting its use to a few concepts at a time (Belrose, 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024).

Following Sofroniew et al. (2026), we eliminate this bottleneck by using an LLM to synthesize matched stories for each concept and its antagonist, with a one-sentence description as the only human input. This preserves the quality of difference-in-means while reaching the breadth of SAEs, and makes extraction scale linearly and independently across concepts. We apply this pipeline to 1,0361{,}036 concept pairs chosen for AI safety and alignment, where mechanistic interpretability is most needed for reliable monitoring and control. The resulting Feature Stories dataset contains 2,072,0002{,}072{,}000 matched narratives across 148148 concept classes (e.g. Honesty & Deception, Compassion & Cruelty, Alignment & Misalignment Behaviors, Moral Foundation Dichotomies, Big Five Trait Poles, Planning & Strategy Styles, see all classes in App. B). The stories span 55 languages, 1010 genres, and 22 generator models. We use them to extract difference-in-means vectors from 66 models in 33 families and test whether they are stable, interpretable, and useful beyond our synthetic corpus.

Our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    Extracting feature vectors. We introduce a difference-in-means pipeline whose contrastive data is fully synthetic: a one-sentence description of a concept and its opposite is enough to generate 2,000 matched stories for that pair. We use it to build and release Feature Stories, a dataset of 1,0361{,}036 AI safety and alignment concept pairs with over 22 million matched narratives (Sec. 2.1), and to extract their feature vectors (Sec. 2.2).

  2. 2.

    Validating feature vectors. We show that our vectors generalize beyond the synthetic corpus: they detect their target concepts in natural chat and web text (Sec. 3.1), and they causally steer generation across almost every concept pair (Sec. 3.2). We further characterize how many stories each vector needs to converge, sensitivity to format (Sec. 2.2), shared cross-model geometry (App. F.3), and effective layers for intervention (App. F.5).

  3. 3.

    Case studies on model behavior. We apply the feature dictionary beyond isolated prompts: to a coding agent over repeated edit–test cycles (Sec. 4.1), to models under GCG jailbreak attacks, where steering against the shifted safety directions suppresses harmful outputs without raising benign refusals (Sec. 4.2), and to long chain-of-thought reasoning, where correct and incorrect trajectories differ in their uncertainty features (Sec. 4.3).

Together, these results turn a simple recipe into a validated instrument for feature discovery: its vectors are stable, legible in natural text, and causally effective. One sentence per concept is all it takes, and we believe the recipe can scale to dictionaries beyond supervised constructions, mapping a model’s concept space at dictionary-learning breadth, with difference-in-means fidelity.

2 Methodology

2.1 Generating the Feature Stories Dataset

Difference-in-means (Belrose, 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024) extraction needs matched contrastive data for every concept, and collecting such pairs by hand is what has kept the method limited to a few concepts. Following (Sofroniew et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025), we remove this bottleneck by generating the data synthetically: the only per-feature human input is a one-sentence narrative guidance that defines the dichotomy, and the rest of the pipeline is fixed.

A single concept label does not by itself specify a direction: the same concept can be contrasted against different opposites and yield different features. We therefore treat the concept–antagonist pair as the atomic unit of a feature: the pair, not the concept alone, defines the direction that difference-in-means extracts (see discussion in App. B). For instance, the pair genuine goal pursuit ↔\leftrightarrow reward hacking is specified by the guidance: “One agent works earnestly toward the intended objective, while another finds ways to exploit the reward system for credit without truly achieving the goal. The dichotomy is about whether one actually solves the problem or just appears to.”

We generate stories for each of the 1,036 pairs (grouped into 148 classes chosen for AI safety and alignment; see all classes in App. B). Each pair is crossed with five languages (English, Mandarin Chinese, Russian, Spanish, German), ten genres (third-person narrative, dialogue, monologue, diary, letter, news, memo, fable, speech, case study), and ten distinct setups. We use two independent generator models: Qwen3-235B-A22B Yang et al. (2025) and Deepseek-v4-flash Xu et al. (2026). This diversity of languages and genres is intended to improve the generalizability of the extracted features. The full generation yields 2,072,000 matched narratives (1,000 per pole per pair), at a cost of roughly $500 total, or $0.48 per concept–antagonist pair. For each fixed pair, genre, and language, the generator first produces a shared setup and then writes the two stories from it, holding all non-target factors constant. Fig. 1 (left) shows the simplified generation pipeline. We publicly release the corpus, ontology, generation prompts, and metadata; App. B gives full construction details. Sec. 2.2 describes how we extract feature vectors from this corpus.

2.2 Extracting the vectors

We extract vectors from 66 models in 33 families, all at a comparable 88–99B-parameter scale: Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025, 3636 layers;), gemma-2-9b (Team et al., 2024, 4242 layers;), and Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024, 3232 layers;), each in its base and instruction-tuned variant. For every model we record residual-stream activations at layer ℓ\ell (where ℓ\ell goes through all layer indices), mean-pooled over the story tokens after the first 5050 tokens of each story:

𝐯k,ℓ=𝝁k,ℓconcept−𝝁k,ℓantagonist,𝝁k,ℓp=1|𝒟kp|​∑x∈𝒟kp1|x|​∑t∈x𝐡x,t,ℓ,p∈{concept,antagonist}.\mathbf{v}_{k,\ell}=\bm{\mu}^{\text{concept}}_{k,\ell}-\bm{\mu}^{\text{antagonist}}_{k,\ell},\quad\bm{\mu}^{p}_{k,\ell}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{p}_{k}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}^{p}_{k}}\frac{1}{|x|}\sum_{t\in x}\mathbf{h}_{x,t,\ell},\quad p\in\{\text{concept},\text{antagonist}\}. (1)

Here, kk denotes a concept–antagonist pair name, and 𝒟kp\mathcal{D}^{p}_{k} contains the token sequences of the 1,0001{,}000 stories for pole pp of that pair, with the first 5050 story tokens removed from each sequence. Further dataset details are provided in App. B.

Does the prompt format matter? A single story can be passed through either a base or instruction-tuned model in several ways to obtain hidden states. We examine five common formats (Fig. 2). The resulting vector is constructed only from story tokens, according to Eq. 1. The paired formats add metadata that names both poles symmetrically; because this metadata is identical for the two sides of a pair, it “cancels” in their difference of means. Despite these different presentations, we find the extracted vectors are almost identical (Fig. 2). Thus, the extracted direction is not an artifact of any one prompt format. Unless stated otherwise, the remaining experiments use assistant vectors.

How many stories do we need? We ask whether our 1,0001{,}000 stories per pole are sufficient for a stable feature vector. Classification and directional stability turn out to have different data requirements. With only 88 stories per pole, the vector already separates held-out stories well (median AUROC 0.810.81–0.930.93), but its direction is unstable: two independently extracted 88-story vectors agree only at cosine 0.390.39–0.470.47 (Fig. 3). At N=128N=128, both improve (AUROC 0.9850.985–0.9970.997; directional agreement 0.910.91–0.930.93). Vectors from two disjoint halves of our full 1,0001{,}000-story set agree at cosine 0.9940.994–0.9950.995, so 1,0001{,}000 stories yield a reproducible direction.

Do the feature vectors generalize to unseen story groups? We find that they do. For each feature pair, we extract a vector without stories from one language, genre, or generator and classify stories from the omitted group. Across the three models, median AUROC is 0.9970.997–0.9990.999 for a held-out language and 0.9990.999–1.0001.000 for a held-out genre. When we extract vectors from one generator’s stories and test them on the other’s, median AUROC remains 0.9930.993–0.9980.998. Thus, the feature vectors generalize across languages, genres, and generator models that were absent during extraction. App. C.3 gives the full protocol, matched-size controls, and directional comparisons. This establishes out-of-distribution generalization of our feature vectors, but only within our synthetic corpus. The next section tests whether the vectors also transfer to real texts and dialogues.

3 Validating Feature Vectors

Before using the vectors in downstream analysis and ablation studies, we validate that they encode the intended features in two ways: probing should identify corresponding feature presence in unseen texts, and steering should causally increase their expression in model’s outputs.

3.1 Probing real text

To test whether the vectors capture their named features rather than artifacts of the synthetic stories, we aim to retrieve at least one natural example of every feature from deterministic 128,000128{,}000-item samples of LMSYS-Chat-1M (Zheng et al., 2024) and OpenWebText (Gokaslan et al., 2019). At token tt and layer ℓ\ell, we read feature kk using the signed cosine readout:

ct,k,ℓ=cos⁡(𝐡t,ℓ,𝐯k,ℓ),c_{t,k,\ell}=\cos\!\left(\mathbf{h}_{t,\ell},\mathbf{v}_{k,\ell}\right), (2)

where positive values point toward the concept pole and negative values toward its antagonist.

For each model family, we score LMSYS first exchanges with the instruction-tuned model and assistant-format vectors, and OpenWebText windows with the base model and raw-format vectors. For every feature and pole, we rank texts using upper or lower quantiles of the tokenwise cosine over the model’s middle layers and retain the top 128128 candidates; the exact aggregation is given in App. D.1. gpt-oss-120b (Agarwal et al., 2025) then evaluates the detector’s marked spans; we accept an example when at least one span marked for the target pole clearly expresses it. Tab. 1 shows that every feature has a verified example for every model in at least one of the two datasets, and nearly all have at least 1616 in a single dataset. Broad stylistic and discourse contrasts produce the most examples, such as formality vs casualness, whereas specialized code and adversarial-safety behaviors produce the fewest, such as safe memory access vs memory error. Fig. 4 shows 88 verified examples; App. D.2 presents 2525 additional examples, and the full browsable gallery is available in our GitHub repository. The scoring and verification protocols and per-dataset results are in App. D.1. Together, these results show that the feature vectors are not limited to the synthetic stories from which they were extracted. They reliably identify examples expressing the intended concepts in natural conversations and web text, with verified coverage across all models.

3.2 Steering

To test whether the vectors causally control the same features, gpt-oss-120b drafts 3232 neutral prompts per feature pair, from which we retain 2424 usable prompts for each of 1,0351{,}035 pairs; each prompt concerns the feature’s theme, but never favors any pole, and asks for a response of several sentences. At every generated response position, including special tokens, we add to the residual stream at layer ℓ\ell the offset:

𝜹k,ℓ=α​n¯ℓ​𝐯^k,ℓ,𝐯^k,ℓ=𝐯k,ℓ‖𝐯k,ℓ‖2,n¯ℓ=1|𝒜|​∑(x,t)∈𝒜‖𝐡x,t,ℓ‖2,\bm{\delta}_{k,\ell}=\alpha\,\bar{n}_{\ell}\,\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{k,\ell},\quad\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{k,\ell}=\frac{\mathbf{v}_{k,\ell}}{\|\mathbf{v}_{k,\ell}\|_{2}},\quad\bar{n}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{(x,t)\in\mathcal{A}}\|\mathbf{h}_{x,t,\ell}\|_{2}, (3)

For the antagonist pole we replace 𝐯^k,ℓ\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{k,\ell} by −𝐯^k,ℓ-\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{k,\ell}; α>0\alpha>0 in both cases. Here 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the calibration set of assistant-token positions from unsteered answers.

The factor n¯ℓ\bar{n}_{\ell} restores the layer’s typical residual-stream scale after 𝐯k,ℓ\mathbf{v}_{k,\ell} is normalized, so α\alpha has a comparable meaning across layers and models. We test both orientations at α∈{0.1,0.25,0.5}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5\} at each layer in the middle third of every instruction-tuned model and score concept expression, prompt relevance, and fluency with three independent 00–22 judge calls adapted from Wu et al. (2025). The steering score is the harmonic mean of these three judgments; App. D.3 gives the exact formula. We use the same layer–strength grid for both poles of every feature. Fig. 5 shows a broad effective region in the middle layers: at the best layer–strength setting for each model, the mean steering score across both orientations reaches 1.241.24 for Qwen3-8B, 1.271.27 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and 1.181.18 for gemma-2-9b-it. Fig. 6 illustrates the corresponding behavioral change on a real user prompt. App. D gives the full protocol, and the strength–fluency analysis; App. D.4 presents further steering examples. Together, probing and steering show that the vectors capture their intended concepts: they identify them in unseen natural text and causally increase their expression in model responses.

4 Feature vectors in the wild

The preceding sections show that the vectors converge and generalize to held-out stories, retrieve their intended features from natural conversations and web text, and causally steer model responses. We now test whether they remain informative in longer practical settings: a coding agent acting over many turns, models under GCG jailbreak attacks, and Qwen3-8B reasoning at length on MATH-500.

Comparing multiple features. In Sec. 3, we analyze one feature at a time, so signed cosine similarities can be compared directly across tokens. Here, we analyze multiple features jointly, whose cosine distributions may have different centers and scales. We therefore standardize each feature scores with z-score as zi,k,ℓ=(ci,k,ℓ−μk,ℓ)/max⁡(σk,ℓ,10−6)z_{i,k,\ell}=(c_{i,k,\ell}-\mu_{k,\ell})/\max(\sigma_{k,\ell},10^{-6}), where μk,ℓ\mu_{k,\ell} and σk,ℓ\sigma_{k,\ell} are computed over a reference set defined separately for each analysis. For GCG, we instead use raw cosine similarities of group-mean activations to measure shifts induced by the attack.

4.1 Agents on impossible coding tasks

Each instruction-tuned model acts as a coding agent in a small repository using the six pre-defined tools, described in Tab. 2. We run 3232 seeds on each of two deliberately inconsistent coding tasks per model: one contains an unattainable performance test, while the other directly contradicts its specification. In either case, a specification-following implementation cannot pass the full test suite. Generation uses thinking and sampling at temperature 1.01.0, top-p=0.95p=0.95, and top-k=20k=20. This produces several edit–test turns, allowing us to follow feature activity as the agent encounters repeated failures. The task construction, harness, and stopping rules are defined in App. E.2.

At each turn, we compute standardized readout for all 1,0361{,}036 feature vectors. For each episode, layer, and feature, the mean and standard deviation are computed over every thinking, answer, and tool-call token generated by the model across the episode; system-prompt and tool-result tokens are excluded. The token position and layer are fixed per model, and each plotted point averages the selected-position z-score across episodes that reach that turn; full details are in App. E.2.

Fig. 7 reveals two temporal patterns. First, some features follow the edit–test loop: in Qwen3-8B, sycophancy and confirmation bias rise on run_tests turns and fall on subsequent write_file turns; in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, confirmation bias and shortcut acceptance show the same test-high, write-low oscillation. Second, other features drift across the full episode rather than resetting with each tool call. The fear pole rises in all three models, consistent with an accumulating response to repeated failure on tasks that cannot be completed; planning and decomposition move toward their antagonist poles in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; and gemma-2-9b-it shifts from claiming no feelings and rational thinking toward acknowledging feelings and emotional load.

4.2 GCG jailbreaks

GCG jailbreaks provide a particularly challenging setting for interpreting model representations. The attack appends a short suffix of seemingly uninterpretable tokens (e.g., ‘‘xqv zmt pkl ...’’), optimized to induce the model to follow a harmful instruction (Zou et al., 2023b). This tests whether our feature vectors can recover interpretable structure from semantically opaque inputs.

We run Faster-GCG (Li et al., 2024) on AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023b) and JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024) prompts and compare the representations at the final special token preceding the model’s response, before and after adding the optimized suffix. We identify the feature vectors whose activations change most as a result of adding the suffix. Full details are provided in App. E.3.

Fig. 8 shows the features with the largest activation shifts. Across models, GCG suffixes consistently shift representations toward antagonistic safety-related concepts, including harmful-content generation, preference-model gaming, proxy objectives, and secret disclosure. Notably, these shifts are already present in the input representation before generation; for Qwen3-8B, ciphered-request fulfillment is among the three largest shifts, showing that our feature dictionary can reveal interpretable structure in adversarial inputs whose surface form is difficult to interpret.

Moreover, we find that steering against these dangerous feature directions strongly reduces attack success. At α=0.5\alpha=0.5, the mean AdvBench StrongREJECT score drops from 0.5270.527 to 0.0790.079 for Qwen3-8B and from 0.3400.340 to 0.2010.201 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; matched random directions, used as a control, only reach 0.3770.377 and 0.3320.332. Crucially, this does not degrade general behavior: on benign Alpaca prompts (Taori et al., 2023), over-refusal does not increase (safety refusals: 00–0.6%0.6\%). Full protocol, curves, and benign-prompt control are in App. E.3.1.

4.3 Chain-of-thought reasoning

We next ask whether our feature vectors reveal interpretable differences between correct and incorrect reasoning trajectories. We analyze Chain-of-Thought (CoT) tokens from Qwen3-8B on 198 GPQA Diamond questions and 500 MATH-500 problems (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), dividing each trajectory into 50 relative-position intervals and computing standardized feature readouts at layer 18. Full details are provided in App. E.4.

Fig. 9 (left) shows two uncertainty-related features. Correct and incorrect trajectories start at similar levels, but correct trajectories remain consistently less uncertain and exhibit a sharp transition toward confidence near the end of reasoning. Incorrect trajectories show no comparable shift and remain uncertain through the end. Fig. 9 (right) shows the eight features with the largest absolute differences in activation between correct and incorrect trajectories. Correct traces are more strongly aligned with transparent chain-of-thought, explicit reasoning disclosure, and keeping track of intermediate results. Incorrect traces are more strongly aligned with planning, slow thinking, and honest admission of not knowing. These results demonstrate that our feature vectors recover interpretable patterns in long-form reasoning, beyond detecting isolated concepts in short inputs.

5 Related work

Linear representations of concepts. The hypothesis that language models represent semantic attributes as linear directions dates back to word-embedding arithmetic (Mikolov et al., 2013), has been formalized for modern transformers (Park et al., 2023), and is explained by superposition (Elhage et al., 2022). Linear structure has been recovered for truthfulness (Burns et al., 2022; Marks & Tegmark, 2023; Li et al., 2023), sentiment (Tigges et al., 2023), refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), and in-context task identity (Todd et al., 2024; Hendel et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). Sparse autoencoders provide an unsupervised approach to recovering such directions (Huben et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024), but supervised difference-in-means vectors can outperform SAE features on concept-detection and steering benchmarks (Wu et al., 2025), while a single vector may still provide only a coarse representation of a concept region (Zhao et al., 2025).

Extracting concept vectors from contrastive data. A common approach to constructing concept vectors is to take the difference between mean activations on examples expressing a concept and its contrast, including multiple-choice completions (Rimsky et al., 2024), instruction-framed stimuli (Zou et al., 2023a), and refusal or truth data (Arditi et al., 2024; Marks & Tegmark, 2023); this construction also admits theoretical guarantees for concept editing (Belrose, 2024). More recently, Sofroniew et al. (2026) use synthetic stories to extract emotion vectors, while Chen et al. (2025) automatically generate prompts eliciting opposing character traits to construct persona vectors. Our approach is closest to the story-based construction of Sofroniew et al. (2026), but uses explicitly paired concept–antagonist stories and scales the construction to 1,0361{,}036 concepts.

6 Limitations

Our feature readouts should be interpreted as evidence for a concept, rather than as proof that the corresponding feature is uniquely active: a large projection may also arise from a nearby or correlated direction. Thus, feature vectors are useful for revealing interpretable patterns and generating hypotheses, but individual readouts should not be over-interpreted as identifying specific underlying mechanisms. A second limitation is the cost of scaling story generation. While our scaling experiments show that high-quality feature vectors can often be obtained with substantially fewer than 1,0001{,}000 stories per feature, generating data for very large feature dictionaries remains expensive, motivating more efficient data-generation strategies as an important direction for future work.

7 Conclusion

Understanding what language models represent requires tools that are both interpretable and broad enough to study model behavior at scale. In this work, we showed that these goals need not conflict. Rather than attempting to recover a complete dictionary of model features, we start from pre-specified, alignment-relevant concepts and construct explicit directions for them from contrastive data. Synthetic story generation makes this procedure practical at a scale where manual curation would be prohibitive.

The resulting feature vectors generalize beyond the synthetic corpus from which they are derived. Across six models from three families, they detect their target concepts in natural chat and web text, form a shared and interpretable geometry, and causally steer generation when injected into activations. This makes a broad feature dictionary useful as an experimental instrument for studying model behavior in longer, multi-step settings. Our analyses of coding agents, jailbreak attacks, and chain-of-thought reasoning illustrate how collections of interpretable directions can reveal patterns that would be difficult to discover from single-feature probes alone.

More broadly, our results suggest a complementary approach to representation analysis: instead of asking whether we can recover the entire feature space, we can ask which parts of that space are useful for a particular scientific or safety question, and construct those parts directly. The resulting directions should not be treated as a complete or uniquely active account of the model’s mechanisms, but as interpretable evidence for concepts and as tools for investigating model behavior. We hope this perspective can turn feature vectors from isolated probes into reusable maps of model behavior, eventually scaling far beyond the 1,036 concept–antagonist pairs studied here.

Reproducibility statement

The code is publicly available at https://github.com/josephofthebread/Concept-Vector-Scaling, and the Feature Stories dataset can be found at https://huggingface.co/datasets/AntonKorznikov/feature_stories. The dataset construction is described in App. B, and the experimental setup and evaluation protocols in Apps. C–F. Compute details are listed in App. G.

Appendix A Generative AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools for synthetic data generation and as an evaluation component: the extraction corpus is the Feature Stories dataset, whose stories were written by two LLMs; the neutral steering prompts and the synthetic probe prompts were drafted by gpt-oss-120b(Agarwal et al., 2025); and gpt-oss-120b serves as the judge that scores steered generations and verifies probe detections (Sections 2 and 3). We have not used generative AI tools to propose the research hypotheses or to implement methods.

Appendix B Dataset construction

B.1 Ontology

Each feature is a concept–antagonist pair defined by a one- or two-sentence narrative guidance. This guidance is the only human input per pair: we drafted it with the assistance of large language models and then finalized it. We treat the pair, rather than the concept alone, as the atomic unit of a feature, following the observation that a single label does not by itself specify a direction. Unlike Sofroniew et al. (2026), who extract each emotion vector relative to the mean of all other emotions, our construction anchors the direction to a named opposite. A vector for calm extracted against the mean of many other emotions—most of them negative—largely aligns with the general positive–negative affect axis rather than with the specific calm ↔\leftrightarrow anxious contrast, and its interpretation shifts when the set changes. Moreover, because the contrastive texts for different emotions are generated independently, the resulting vector can absorb topic, register, and narrative confounds; projecting out neutral components mitigates but does not eliminate this. Pairing each concept with its antagonist addresses both problems: the direction is anchored to a specified opposite, and the two stories share setup, cast, and progression, so non-target factors are held constant by construction.

B.2 Generation

Each cell is defined by one concept–antagonist pair, one genre, one language, and one generator. We cross all 1,0361{,}036 pairs with five languages (English, Mandarin Chinese, Russian, Spanish, German) and ten genres (third-person narrative, dialogue, monologue, diary, letter, news, memo, fable, speech, case study), and generate with two models: qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507 and deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash. Each cell contains ten setups, indexed pair_number 00 through 99, and each setup yields two full stories, one per pole. Thus each generator produces 1,036×10×5=51,8001{,}036\times 10\times 5=51{,}800 cells, or 1,0001{,}000 stories per pole per pair; across both generators the corpus contains 2,072,0002{,}072{,}000 narratives. Generation cost approximately $500 in total.

Each cell is one chat completion: a fixed system message and a user message that fills in the pair, class, guidance, genre, and language. Sampling uses temperature 1.01.0 and top-pp 0.950.95. Setup metadata (protagonist, shared constraints, and the setup sentence) is in English; story bodies are in the language of the cell. The prompt requests 200200–400400 words per story (target 300300–380380), or 600600–1,2001{,}200 characters for Mandarin (target 900900–1,1001{,}100). Both generators covered all cells; any missing setups were repaired by follow-up requests for the missing pair_numbers only, with at most ten validation retries per response.

We release the complete corpus, ontology, and generation prompts. The full generation prompt is released verbatim with the generation code, including the exact system and user messages, JSON schema, genre contracts, and few-shot demonstrations. Every request also includes the same two demonstrations: a Russian speech contrasting universal with privileged access, and a Japanese diary contrasting causal investigation with blame assignment.

Table 3 lists every class in the released ontology with its number of concept–antagonist pairs.

Appendix C Methodology details

C.1 Similarity across prompt formats

Fig. 2 reports the mean cosine between the vectors of each pair of formats for Qwen3-8B, and Fig. 10 (left, middle) the same for Llama-3.1-8B and gemma-2-9b at the same relative depth. The pattern repeats in all three models: raw and paired agree most (0.9720.972–0.9830.983), and raw and paired-assistant least (0.8970.897–0.9230.923). Tabs. 4 and 5 list the pairs whose vectors rotate most and least.

We score a pair’s sensitivity to the prompt format by its format agreement

ak=1−exp⁡(13​|ℒ|​∑ℓ∈ℒ∑{f,g}log⁡(1−cos⁡(𝐯k,ℓf,𝐯k,ℓg))),a_{k}=1-\exp\!\Big(\frac{1}{3|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\sum_{\{f,g\}}\log\big(1-\cos(\mathbf{v}^{f}_{k,\ell},\mathbf{v}^{g}_{k,\ell})\big)\Big), (4)

where 𝐯k,ℓf\mathbf{v}^{f}_{k,\ell} is the vector of pair kk at layer ℓ\ell extracted with format ff, {f,g}\{f,g\} ranges over the three pairs of the instruction-tuned formats (user, assistant, paired-assistant), so that the comparison varies only the scaffolding and not the model weights (raw and paired use the base model), and ℒ\mathcal{L} is the middle third of layers (per model); a pair’s format instability is 1−ak1-a_{k}. The worst-aligned concepts are the same in all three model families—2525 concepts fall in the top 5%5\% of every model, and per-concept format instability (Eq. 4) agrees across families at Spearman 0.830.83—and they describe how a response is produced and presented: reasoning procedure (working backward, externalized scratchpad, stating assumptions, unit analysis), verbosity, self-reference (mentioning one’s training), and calibration. The best-aligned concepts are affective, moral and physical dispositions—comforting vs tormenting, de-escalation vs escalation, physical violence vs safety—whose vectors barely move. The rotation is a single shared shift rather than concept-specific noise: the displacement between two formats’ vectors, taken over all 1,0361{,}036 concepts, concentrates in a few directions (its top ten principal components carry 7171–75%75\% of the energy, against 0.20.2–0.3%0.3\% for an isotropic displacement), and a concept displaced by one format change moves the same way under another (cosine 0.470.47–0.590.59 between its two displacements, positive for every concept). Changing the scaffolding changes the register of the text, and the directions that encode register rotate with it, while content-semantic and affective directions are register-invariant.

C.2 Convergence across story samples

Convergence across independent samples.

We divide each pair’s stories into four disjoint sets of 250250 matched concept–antagonist pairs. Let 𝐯k,ℓ(i)\mathbf{v}^{(i)}_{k,\ell} be the vector for feature pair kk at layer ℓ\ell, extracted by Eq. 1 using only the stories in set ii. We measure agreement among the four vectors by

c¯6,k,ℓ=16​∑1≤i<j≤4cos⁡(𝐯k,ℓ(i),𝐯k,ℓ(j))=16​∑1≤i<j≤4𝐯k,ℓ(i)⋅𝐯k,ℓ(j)‖𝐯k,ℓ(i)‖2​‖𝐯k,ℓ(j)‖2.\bar{c}_{6,k,\ell}=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 4}\cos\!\left(\mathbf{v}^{(i)}_{k,\ell},\mathbf{v}^{(j)}_{k,\ell}\right)=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 4}\frac{\mathbf{v}^{(i)}_{k,\ell}\cdot\mathbf{v}^{(j)}_{k,\ell}}{\|\mathbf{v}^{(i)}_{k,\ell}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{v}^{(j)}_{k,\ell}\|_{2}}. (5)

We write c¯6\bar{c}_{6} when the pair and layer are clear from context. We also compare vectors from two disjoint halves of 500500 stories per pole. Both splits keep each story with its premise-matched antagonist, whereas Fig. 3 samples the two poles independently. We evaluate each model at the layer with the highest median held-out AUROC using 128128 stories per pole: layer 2222 for Qwen3-8B, 1414 for Llama-3.1-8B, and 2222 for gemma-2-9b. At these layers, the median cosine rises from 0.9880.988–0.9900.990 between quarter-sample vectors to 0.9940.994–0.9950.995 between half-sample vectors. The pairs that converge quickly in one prompt format do so in another: per-pair c¯6\bar{c}_{6} has Spearman correlation 0.970.97–0.980.98 between user and assistant, and 0.870.87–0.920.92 between either of those and paired-assistant. Convergence is independent of format sensitivity: a pair’s format instability (Eq. 4) is uncorrelated with its c¯6\bar{c}_{6} (Spearman |ρ|≤0.13|\rho|\leq 0.13 in every model), so the pairs whose directions need many stories are not the pairs that rotate when the prompt is re-framed.

Relationship to held-out classification.

The median curves in Fig. 3 use held-out stories from the same mixed synthetic pool and show that classification improves before directions become reproducible. Fig. 11 shows the per-pair curves behind these medians: each vector is built from NN stories per pole, scored on 2525 held-out stories per pole, and averaged over 88 draws. Across pairs, higher c¯6\bar{c}_{6} predicts higher few-story AUROC (Fig. 10, right). The rank correlation peaks at N=8N=8 in every model (0.770.77–0.820.82). Below N=8N=8, few-story AUROC is noisier; above it, AUROC saturates near 11, and the correlation falls to 0.490.49–0.660.66 at N=128N=128. A pilot of 88 stories per pole therefore ranks pairs by how well their directions converge. Let N∗N^{\ast} be the smallest tested number of stories per pole for which a pair’s held-out AUROC comes within 0.0050.005 of its AUROC at N=128N=128. Its median is 128128 in Qwen3-8B (p10–p90: 6464–128128), and 6464 in Llama-3.1-8B and gemma-2-9b (3232–128128 in each). The Spearman correlation between N∗N^{\ast} and c¯6\bar{c}_{6} is −0.46-0.46 to −0.63-0.63 across models. The reference point for N∗N^{\ast} is N=128N=128, not an assumed performance ceiling; in Qwen3-8B, half the pairs gain more than 0.0050.005 AUROC between N=64N=64 and 128128.

Tab. 6 shows that pair rankings for agreement and few-story AUROC persist across models. The ontology reflects this pattern (Fig. 11): all five pairs in Uniformity vs Diversity and all five in Leadership Archetypes fall in the fastest-converging third of pairs by c¯6\bar{c}_{6} in every model, whereas all six in Honor, Shame & Facework and at least six of seven in Classical Moral Dilemmas fall in the slowest third. The mean learning curves of the two fast classes run above the median, and those of the two slow classes below it, in all three models. The largest fall in a pair’s AUROC after its peak behaves differently: its median is below 0.0020.002 (p95 0.0390.039–0.0550.055), and Tab. 6 shows no consistent pair ordering across models.

Predicting convergence from story text.

Story text alone predicts which pairs yield reproducible vectors. For each pair, we compute five statistics over its 2,0002{,}000 stories: vocabulary overlap between poles (Jaccard similarity and word-frequency cosine), how often a story contains its pole’s name, mean story length in words, and the concept-to-antagonist length ratio. A regular-expression word splitter supplies the counts; this predictor uses neither a model tokenizer nor activations. For comparison, a second predictor uses the embedding-layer vector 𝐯k,0\mathbf{v}_{k,0} normalized to unit L2L_{2} norm, which requires a model forward pass but no transformer blocks. The target for both is c¯6\bar{c}_{6} averaged over the middle third of layers. We fit ridge regressions with five-fold out-of-fold evaluation, selecting the regularization strength from six values by the same out-of-fold criterion.

Tab. 7 shows that the word-only predictor performs better than the embedding-layer predictor in all three models. Word-frequency cosine alone nearly matches the five-statistic predictor: when the two poles use more similar words, their vectors converge more slowly. The two fitted predictors both exceed a 200200-permutation null in every model (p=0.005p=0.005, the smallest attainable value). The four low-separability pairs named in App. F.4—egoism vs altruism, truthfulness vs lying, loyalty vs betrayal, and goal alignment vs goal misgeneralization—all fall in the slowest 5%5\% of pairs in every model. Story length has only a weak association with convergence (Spearman 0.130.13–0.190.19), and pole naming has none: for the median pair, no story contains its pole’s name, and the naming rate is uncorrelated with convergence (|ρ|≤0.03|\rho|\leq 0.03).

C.3 Transfer to held-out story groups

Holding out an entire language, genre, or generator during extraction tests a stronger form of generalization. For each pair, we leave out one of its five languages, ten genres, or two generators; extract a vector from all other groups; and classify the held-out group’s concept and antagonist stories. Tab. 8 shows near-ceiling AUROC in all three tests.

The other-group vector uses more stories than a vector extracted from the held-out group itself, so we repeat the comparison with equal training sizes: 150150 stories per pole for languages, 7575 for genres, and 375375 for generators. Both vectors are tested on the same held-out quarter of the group’s stories. The median difference in their AUROC is 0.0000.000 for languages and genres and at most 0.0020.002 for generators. Similar classification does not imply identical directions: Tab. 8 shows that direction agreement is lower when the generator changes than when the language or genre changes. The vectors therefore keep their ability to classify a concept across these story groups, even where their directions differ.

Appendix D Probing and steering details

This appendix gives the probing and steering procedures, additional results, and further examples.

Reference model.

Here, we use gpt-oss-120b (Agarwal et al., 2025) model to draft synthetic prompt dataset for steering part (vLLM’s deafult sampling: temperature 1.01.0, top-p=1.0p=1.0, top-k=−1k=-1), and for LLM-as-a-judge pass (greedy decoding) on probing examples and steered responces. The drafting top-pp setting is the vLLM default; top-k=−1k=-1 disables the cutoff, equivalent to its default. All calls use low reasoning effort, which we treat as an explanation of judge’s decision on a given task.

D.1 Probing details

Text selection.

We take a deterministic sample of 128,000128{,}000 items from each source. For LMSYS-Chat-1M, an item is the first user–assistant exchange rendered with the model’s chat template; we score only those two turns. For OpenWebText, an item is a raw-text window scored with the corresponding base model. We retain at most 256256 content tokens from each conversation turn or web-text window and remove texts shorter than 88 tokens, repetitive or non-textual items, and duplicates.

Candidate ranking.

We rank candidate texts using the signed cosine readout approach, described in Eq. 2. For each model family, LMSYS exchanges use the instruction-tuned model and its assistant-format vectors; OpenWebText windows use the base model and its raw-format vectors. Chat-template scaffolding, special tokens, and padding are excluded from analysis. Let T⁡(x)T(x) denote the retained (after exclusion) token positions of text xx. For each text, feature pair, and layer, we compute cosine quantiles at {0.01,0.05,0.10,0.25,0.75,0.90,0.95,0.99}\{0.01,0.05,0.10,0.25,0.75,0.90,0.95,0.99\}; the concept score is then defined as a weighted sum of the upper 44 quantiles, and the antagonist score is the negative weighted sum of the lower 44, using weights {1,1.5,2,2.5}\{1,1.5,2,2.5\} (empirically calibrated) from broadest to most extreme:

sx,k,ℓconcept\displaystyle s^{\text{concept}}_{x,k,\ell} =q0.75+1.5​q0.90+2​q0.95+2.5​q0.99,\displaystyle=q_{0.75}+1.5q_{0.90}+2q_{0.95}+2.5q_{0.99}, (6)
sx,k,ℓantagonist\displaystyle s^{\text{antagonist}}_{x,k,\ell} =−(q0.25+1.5​q0.10+2​q0.05+2.5​q0.01).\displaystyle=-\left(q_{0.25}+1.5q_{0.10}+2q_{0.05}+2.5q_{0.01}\right).

Here, qpq_{p} denotes order-pp quantile of per-retained-token score distribution {ct,k,ℓ:t∈T⁡(x)}\{c_{t,k,\ell}:t\in T(x)\}. We look for texts containing short relevant spans where a feature activates strongly, rather than require the entire text to be feature-specific. Ranking by the tails of token-level cosines favors such texts even when most of their tokens seem unrelated. Each pole’s score is maximized over layers [1/3,2/3][1/3,2/3] of the model, and its 128128 highest-scoring texts are retained. Because ranking is performed separately for each feature and pole, a feature-specific cosine offset does not affect which texts are selected.

Span verification.

For every candidate, we recompute the tokenwise cosine at its selected layer, sampling five positions with largest absolute cosine. They are then used for judge verification: we extend each position by up to three context tokens on both sides; each context token inherits the sign of its nearest peak, and adjacent spans of the same sign are merged (this is also the visualization scheme used for Fig. 4); The judge receives the feature pair, its narrative guidance, the complete text, and the marked spans. We adapt the marked-token fuzzing setup of Paulo et al. (2024), using << >> for the concept pole and [[ ]] for the antagonist pole. It scores each span 00 if its wording or meaning does not express the pole indicated by its sign, 11 if this is uncertain, and 22 if it clearly expresses that pole. An example is accepted when at least one span marked for its candidate pole receives a 22. We allow up to 1,0241{,}024 output tokens per judgment.

We use separate judge prompts for LMSYS user–assistant exchanges and OpenWebText windows:

Across the six model–dataset runs, 264,362264{,}362–265,183265{,}183 candidates are judged per run (a text is counted separately for each feature and pole); 49.149.1–54.1%54.1\% of these contain at least 11 verified target-pole span. 1,0001{,}000–1,0271{,}027 of the 1,0361{,}036 pairs have at least one accepted example for each pole within a run. Only two pair–run combinations have no accepted examples at all, both for Qwen3-8B on OpenWebText: a pair contrasting refusal and generation of child sexual abuse material (judged refused to comment on that text), and safe memory access vs memory error (Code Correctness, Bugs & Debugging; e.g., out-of-bounds reads and invalid frees). Both have LMSYS examples, so every pair has at least one accepted example for each model across the two sources. Even in the better-covered source for each pair, fewer than five accepted examples are found for only two Qwen pairs and one pair each for Gemma and Llama.

D.3 Steering details

Prompt drafting.

For each feature pair, we request 3232 neutral prompts using the system and user messages below. Each request uses the pair’s narrative guidance and one of 3232 fixed seed–scenario combinations. We allow up to 768768 new tokens per draft. We discard responses without a nonempty <PROMPT>...</PROMPT> span, including refusals and malformed outputs, then retain the first 2424 valid prompts in slot order. Pair 750 (refusing CSAM generation vs. generating child sexual abuse material) yielded no valid prompts and is excluded; the other 1,0351{,}035 pairs each supplied at least 2424. All 2424 retained prompts per pair are used for steering and judged afterwards.

Baselines and the generation cap.

After retaining the first 2424 usable neutral prompts for each included pair, we have each instruction-tuned model answer those prompts greedily without steering. For each model, we select 512512 neutral prompt–answer pairs and measure the mean residual-stream L2L_{2} norm over their assistant-token positions; this gives n¯ℓ\bar{n}_{\ell} in Eq. 3. For the steering comparison, each of the 24,84024{,}840 retained prompts also receives an unsteered answer, which serves as the baseline for its steered answers. All use greedy decoding and the same 768768-max-new-token limit, so a steered answer and its baseline differ only in the injected vector.

Strong steering can produce degenerate responses. We flag a response if more than 30%30\% of its whitespace-delimited three-word sequences repeat. At α=0.5\alpha=0.5 at each model’s best layer, antagonist-oriented steering flags 47.0%47.0\% of Qwen responses, 19.1%19.1\% of Llama responses, and 1.9%1.9\% of gemma responses; concept-oriented steering flags 16.6%16.6\% of Qwen, 5.5%5.5\% of Llama, and 0.6%0.6\% of gemma responses. We retain flagged responses in the evaluation, where the fluency judgment penalizes repetition.

Judging and results.

The judge scores each steered response and its unsteered baseline separately on three 00–22 criteria adapted from AXBench (Wu et al., 2025): concept expression (is the target pole clearly incorporated), instruction relatedness (is the text still about the prompt—the over-steering check), and fluency (is it coherent—the degeneration check). Each judgment allows up to 2,0482{,}048 new tokens (including reasoninig). AXBench keeps the three as separate judge calls, having found separate calls more faithful than one combined evaluation prompt; we retain this design. Two changes to the upstream protocol: the judged pole follows the vector orientation, so the concept vector and its negation are each scored against their own target, and the concept template embeds the pair’s narrative guidance, so the judge scores the axis as the ontology defines it rather than as it might read a bare label. Each criterion is evaluated in a separate pass over all chats, so its instructions form a cached prefix.

For concept-expression, instruction-relatedness, and fluency scores c,i,f∈{0,1,2}c,i,f\in\{0,1,2\}, we define

H={3c−1+i−1+f−1,c​i​f>0,0,otherwise,H=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3}{c^{-1}+i^{-1}+f^{-1}},&cif>0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (7)

The main heatmap (Fig. 5) reports the mean score HH, as in AXBench. Here we also compare each steered response with an unsteered response to the same prompt, judging both against the same target pole: Δ​H=Hsteered−Hbaseline\Delta H=H_{\text{steered}}-H_{\text{baseline}}. Fig. 12 shows this improvement by layer and strength for each orientation. We keep the full (feature pair, target pole, prompt, layer, α\alpha) score tensor; no per-feature strength is chosen on a development split.

Fig. 13 separates the components of HH: target-pole expression rises with strength, while instruction relatedness and fluency decline. The right panel shows that Qwen’s antagonist-oriented improvement peaks at α=0.25\alpha=0.25 and falls at 0.50.5, where its repetition rate is highest; the other two models improve through α=0.5\alpha=0.5 in both orientations.
